title: Turmeric Is 2026's Herb of the Year — And India's Pantry Staples Are Conquering American Wellness Culture
excerpt: From ghee in coffee to A2 cow ghee on fitness influencer feeds, traditional Indian superfoods are riding a wellness wave that would make your grandmother say 'I told you so.'
body:
Every Indian kitchen has had a jar of turmeric on the shelf for as long as anyone can remember. Now the rest of America is catching up. The International Herb Association named turmeric the 2026 Herb of the Year, formally recognising what Ayurvedic practitioners have known for millennia: this unassuming golden rhizome is a powerhouse.

## The Science Catches Up to the Kitchen

Turmeric's moment is not purely cultural. A growing body of modern research supports its role in reducing inflammation, supporting joint health, and potentially aiding cognitive function. The American College of Healthcare Sciences notes that turmeric "bridges ancient wisdom and modern science," with applications ranging from standardised supplements to topical preparations and essential oil blends.

The key active compound, curcumin, has been the subject of thousands of peer-reviewed studies. One practical finding that would delight any Indian grandmother: combining turmeric with black pepper — as in traditional haldi doodh — dramatically increases curcumin absorption. The evening ritual of turmeric milk, once dismissed as old-fashioned, is now being rebranded as a "potent immunity shot" by Western nutritionists.

## Ghee's Remarkable Second Act

If turmeric is having a moment, ghee is having a full-blown renaissance. The clarified butter that was demonised during America's low-fat craze is now a wellness darling. In 2026, "ghee in coffee" has become one of the year's breakout wellness trends, with health influencers touting its benefits for gut health, brain function, and sustained energy.

The numbers are striking. Organic Valley, a farmer-owned cooperative, reported a 25 per cent increase in ghee sales in 2025. The flavoured ghee market is expanding rapidly, with brands launching garlic and turmeric infusions, single-serve pods, and millet-based pairings. Amul, India's most recognisable dairy brand, is exploring entry into North American markets through partnerships with regional retailers.

A2 cow ghee — made from the milk of indigenous Indian cow breeds — has become particularly popular among fitness enthusiasts. Social media influencers promoting clean eating, traditional nutrition, and Ayurvedic wellness have driven awareness among younger consumers who might never have encountered ghee in their parents' kitchens.

## The Broader Indian Superfoods Wave

Turmeric and ghee are not alone. A constellation of Indian pantry staples is migrating from diaspora kitchens to mainstream American shelves. Makhana (fox nuts) is being marketed as a high-protein, low-calorie snack. Millets — which India championed at the United Nations in 2023 — continue to gain traction in health food stores. Amla (Indian gooseberry) is appearing in supplement aisles, and jaggery is being positioned as a less-processed alternative to refined sugar.

The demand has evolved beyond basic staples. Today's Indian-American consumer — and increasingly, the non-Indian wellness consumer — wants region-specific products, Ayurvedic formulations, and authentic preparations. Online searches for "Indian products USA" have surged, pushing retailers and e-commerce platforms to rethink their offerings.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

There is something bittersweet about watching the foods you grew up eating become someone else's wellness trend. The turmeric your mother pressed onto every scrape is now a $3 latte add-on. The ghee your grandmother insisted was essential is now a premium product with a minimalist label and a yoga-adjacent brand name.

But there is validation too. For NRIs who spent years explaining why their food smelled different, watching American wellness culture embrace the Indian pantry feels like a long-overdue acknowledgment. As one viral social media post put it: your grandma was not doing Ayurveda. She was just making dinner.
author: Diaspora Desk
